### Related literature {#sec-literature}

The real-options foundation rests on @mcdonald1986value for optimal timing of irreversible investment and @pindyck1988irreversible for capacity choice. @guo2005investment model demand with regime-dependent drift and volatility, showing large investment jumps on favorable regime arrival; @decamps2006irreversible study the choice between two irreversible projects of different scale under a single geometric Brownian output price, with an extension in which the firm may later switch from the smaller to the larger project; the present paper's scale choice is in that tradition, while its $L \to H$ transition is an exogenous Poisson regime switch rather than a project switch chosen by the firm. Neither includes strategic interaction, training-inference allocation, or default risk. The capacity-choice problem is also studied in operations management [@vanmieghem2003capacity], whose closest construct is resource flexibility: @chod2005resource show that a flexible resource allocated across products *after* demand is observed substitutes for capacity. Compute is flexible in that sense, but the allocation here is a commitment made at installation whose training component pays off only in a different demand regime, and it is priced jointly with the firm's default decision.

Strategic real-options models replace the single decision maker with rivals whose entry erodes the option value of waiting [@grenadier2002option]. The closest strategic-investment paper is @huisman2015strategic, who study a duopoly with joint timing and capacity choice; I extend their framework with endogenous default risk, training-inference allocation, diminishing returns, and regime switching. @aguerrevere2003equilibrium and @aguerrevere2009real link installed capacity and competitive intensity to the composition of firm value between assets in place and growth options, and hence to expected returns, an antecedent of the training-beta conjecture of @sec-discussion; here the risk composition shifts with the *split* of a given capacity rather than with its level. @lambrecht2003real study duopoly real options under incomplete information, where firms hold private signals about the payoff, related to the heterogeneous beliefs about the AGI arrival rate $\lambda$ here but without the allocation or default mechanisms.

The paper also connects to patent races and R&D competition. @loury1979market and @reinganum1982strategic model firms choosing R&D intensity to accelerate a stochastic Poisson breakthrough, and @harris1987racing derive a discouragement effect for lagging firms that echoes the follower's delayed entry in the duopoly equilibrium; in the present model position affects the allocation only modestly, since the leader's training fraction lies $3.1\%$ below the single firm's at baseline (Proposition 3(ii)). @weeds2002strategic places a winner-take-all patent race in a real-options duopoly with irreversible investment and shows that competition can delay rather than hasten investment; the entry game here has a related feature, a second-mover advantage at the date of first investment, although competition still brings that date forward of the switch. The key departure is the dual role of capacity: in standard races, investment during the race is pure cost, whereas here installed capacity generates inference revenue before AGI arrives and training quality determines position afterwards.

The firm's default decision follows the structural credit-risk tradition of @merton1974pricing and @leland1994corporate, a literature that already embeds regime switching in the Leland framework. @hackbarth2006capital let cash flows depend on a two-state macroeconomic regime and derive default and financing policies that adapt to the cycle; @chen2010macroeconomic and @bhamra2010levered add a consumption-based pricing kernel. Proposition 2 is therefore not the first default boundary derived in a regime-switching environment; those papers in fact solve the fully coupled system with regime-contingent boundaries, whereas @eq-default-boundary uses a single boundary that embeds the switch in unconditional expectation (@sec-model documents the resulting approximation error; the entry equilibrium and the credit exhibits use the coupled boundaries). The Leland framework suits public-debt issuers; for the VC-backed archetypes in the calibration, "default" should be read broadly as financial distress (failed funding round, liquidity crisis), consistent with @gornall2020squaring.

The model's technology assumptions come from the economics of AI. Training exhibits power-law scaling [@kaplan2020scaling; @hoffmann2022training], motivating the concave production function, and @agrawal2019economics frame AI as a prediction technology connecting inference demand to value creation. @aghion2019artificial, @acemoglu2024simple, @korinek2024scenarios, and @jones2024agi analyze the growth implications of transformative AI in general equilibrium; the present paper is partial equilibrium and complements them with a firm-level investment and allocation problem. On the allocation margin itself, the closest analog is @akcigit2018growth on exploitation versus exploration R&D, set in a multi-product firm rather than in a compute allocation problem.

The marginal contribution is a set of results the closest models do not generate. In the papers that combine irreversible investment with endogenous default [@mauer2005real; @hackbarth2014capital; @sundaresan2015dynamic; @kumar2018optimal], installed capital is homogeneous, so the firm has no decision that trades current revenue against the value of surviving to a later regime. The training fraction $\phi$ is that decision here. Its optimum has a closed form that rises with the arrival rate and does not depend on scale (Proposition 1), and it governs how the default boundary responds to beliefs: above a closed-form threshold, a higher arrival rate lowers the boundary through the expected post-AGI continuation value (*faith-based survival*, whose thresholds are @eq-phi-underbar and @eq-phi-tilde). The same margin carries the expected-value cost of a mistaken belief in *Dario's dilemma*. The allocation is the largest component of the loss on both sides, and it is the main reason a pessimistic error costs more than an optimistic one of the same size in $\lambda$ (Numerical Finding 1). Default and recovery shape where the tail risk falls, and less than one might expect: the boundary that matters is created by operating costs without any debt, leverage shifts it, and recovery is small and weakly increasing in the training fraction at the model's policies, so the continuation value that keeps the firm alive adds nothing to what creditors recover and takes nothing from it. On timing, the strategic real-options models above obtain early investment from a race to be first. Here a single firm that chooses its scale at the switch waits for it at baseline, competition is what brings investment forward of the switch, and at the date of first investment following is the better role (Proposition 3). The regime-switching credit models take the size of the growth option as exogenous, so the firm cannot buy survival by sacrificing current revenue, and the allocation problems closest in structure [@akcigit2018growth; @chod2005resource] are solved for firms whose survival is not at stake. The investment-financing framework follows @hackbarth2012corporate.
